reason: The text consistently portrays the Hebrews as a structured nation rather than merely a family or religious adherents. Multiple linguistic and structural markers support this: (1) repeated use of עַם (am/people) and בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (collective identity); (2) administrative hierarchy shown through נֹגְשִׂים (taskmasters) and שֹׁטְרִים (officers), indicating organized governance; (3) territorial association with אֶרֶץ גֹּשֶׁן (land of Goshen); (4) Pharaoh's interaction treats them as a subject people requiring labor administration, not a family; (5) their collective exemption from certain plagues (the hail) demonstrates distinct national/territorial status; (6) the reference to אֱלֹהֵ֣י הָעִבְרִ֔ים (God of the Hebrews) emphasizes corporate religious identity. The text systematically presents them as עַם (a people/nation) with institutional organization, geographic location, and political status—characteristics that transcend family kinship or individual religious adherence.
